pos: n. (Laurence Humphrey, c. 1527–1589, Marian exile, President of Magdalen College, Oxford)
etymology: Latin Laurentius, crowned with laurel; Germanic Hunfrid, peace of the Hun, giant-peace.
biblical_def: Laurence Humphrey was a Cambridge fellow who left England when Mary Tudor came to the throne, spent the years of exile at Zurich, Basel and Geneva, and came home at Elizabeth's accession to spend the rest of his life as President of Magdalen College, Oxford, and in the end Dean of Winchester. He is remembered chiefly for what he would not do. With Thomas Sampson he refused to wear the surplice and the square cap, holding that garments borrowed from the Roman mass could not be made indifferent by an act of state, and he was disciplined for it while the vestiarian controversy ran its course. The dictionary does not treat that quarrel as a matter of taste. Humphrey's argument was that a church which had buried the mass should not keep its clothes, and that a conscience bound by Scripture cannot be unbound by a royal injunction. He also wrote the first life of Bishop Jewel and a treatise on nobility which located true greatness in godliness rather than blood, and he filled Magdalen with preachers. He was a scholar who had seen the Reformed churches of the Rhine at close quarters and never afterward thought England had gone far enough.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines exile as banishment, and nonconformity as refusal of compliance with an established usage.
webster_full: EX'ILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country.
NONCONFORM'ITY, n. Neglect or failure of conformity; in England, the refusal to unite with the established church.
PRES'IDENT, n. An officer appointed to preside over a college or society.
CON'SCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge; the faculty, power or principle which decides on the lawfulness or unlawfulness of our actions.
scriptures: Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
And he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin.
Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.

For our rejoicing is this, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world, and more abundantly to you-ward.
corruption_summary: He would not wear the mass vestments, and said a conscience bound by Scripture cannot be unbound by statute.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern habit of filing every scruple about worship under personality — the high churchman likes ceremony, the low churchman does not, and both are served. Humphrey held that the question was not taste but authority: who may bind the worship of God, and on what warrant. Having lived in Zurich and seen a church ordered simply, he came back unable to pretend that the surplice was nothing.

The principle to recover is that conscience answers to God before it answers to the magistrate, and that this is not rebellion but the order of things. “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). The man who acts against his own judgment in worship is not thereby obedient: “for whatsoever is not of faith is sin” (Rom 14:23). And the reward of such a course is not comfort but a clear testimony — “the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity” (2Co 1:12).

pos: n. (John Pullain, c. 1517–1565, Marian exile, minister of the English congregation at Geneva, psalm-versifier)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan through Latin Johannes, the LORD is gracious; Pullain, from Old French poulain, a colt.
biblical_def: John Pullain was an Oxford man and rector of St Peter's Cornhill in London who, when Mary came in, did not immediately run. He stayed and preached to those who would gather, and only afterward made his way abroad, where with Christopher Goodman he served the English congregation at Geneva that Knox had helped to shape. There he put Psalms into English metre for the exiles to sing, and some of his versions passed into the psalters the returning congregations used. At Elizabeth's accession he came home and was made archdeacon of Colchester. The dictionary holds him up for the pairing: a pastor who both preached under threat and set the Psalms to a tune his people could carry out of the country with them. The exiles had lost their parishes, their livings and their land; what they could not be deprived of was the Psalter in their own mouths. Pullain's labour belongs to the same recovery as the translators' — the conviction that the word of God is given to a congregation to be understood, spoken and sung, not performed over them in a tongue they do not have.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines psalm as a sacred song, and metre as the measured arrangement of syllables in verse.
webster_full: PSALM, n. A sacred song or hymn; a song composed on a divine subject and in praise of God.
ME'TRE, n. Rhythmical arrangement of syllables or words into verses, stanzas, strophes.
ARCHDE'ACON, n. In England, an ecclesiastical dignitary next in rank below a bishop.
CONGREGA'TION, n. A collection or assembly of separate things; an assembly of persons met for the worship of God.
scriptures: How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Praise ye the LORD. Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise in the congregation of saints.
And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them.
corruption_summary: He preached under Mary, then put the Psalms into English metre for the exiles at Geneva to sing.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the treatment of congregational singing as a department of taste, staffed by the musically able and judged by the pleasure it gives. Pullain versified Psalms for people who had no instruments, no building and no country. The question before him was not what would move a congregation but what God had given a congregation to sing.

The principle to recover is that the Psalter is the church's own songbook and travels with her. The exiles' question was the right one — “How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?” (Psa 137:4) — and the answer was to sing it anyway. Paul and Silas had already settled the matter in a prison at Philippi, and the apostolic command is plain: “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16).

pos: n. (Thomas Bentham, 1513–1579, pastor of the London underground congregation under Mary, afterwards Bishop of Coventry and Lichfield)
etymology: Aramaic Te'oma through Greek Thomas, a twin; English Bentham, the homestead among the bent grass.
biblical_def: Thomas Bentham was expelled from Magdalen College under Mary, went into exile at Zurich and Basel, and then did the thing the exiles mostly did not do: he went back. From about 1557 he served as pastor of the secret Protestant congregation in London, meeting in houses and fields while the fires at Smithfield were still burning, and he is reported to have stood up at one burning and called the crowd to pray for the sufferers. At Elizabeth's accession he was made Bishop of Coventry and Lichfield, a poor and scattered diocese, and worked it for twenty years. The dictionary holds him up as the plainest answer to the charge that the Marian exiles saved themselves. Bentham had the safety of Zurich and left it, by his own reckoning because a congregation in England had no minister. His pastorate was illegal, unpaid and hunted, and it kept a church together in the capital until the queen died. The shepherd who goes toward the danger because the sheep are in it is the biblical pattern, and he is one of its clearest English instances.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pastor as a minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church, and oversight as watchful care.
webster_full: P'ASTOR, n. A minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church and congregation.
O'VERSIGHT, n. Superintendence; watchful care; as the oversight of a flock.
CONVEN'TICLE, n. An assembly or meeting; appropriately, a secret or unlawful assembly for religious worship.
DI'OCESE, n. The circuit or extent of a bishop's jurisdiction.
scriptures: I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
Heb 13:3
Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body.
corruption_summary: He left the safety of Zurich to pastor the hunted London congregation while Mary reigned.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a view of ministry as a post rather than a charge — something one holds while conditions allow and resigns when they do not. Bentham had been deprived of everything a post can give and went back to the work without any of it, in a city where preaching the gospel was a capital matter.

The principle to recover is that the shepherd is bound to the flock and not to the salary. “I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep” (Joh 10:11). Peter's charge assumes that the oversight will cost something and is to be taken up willingly all the same: “not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2). And the command to the church about her prisoners is to feel it in the body — “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them” (Heb 13:3).

pos: n. (Richard Chambers, d. 1566, layman, treasurer and almoner of the Marian exile congregations)
etymology: Germanic Ricohard, strong in rule; English Chambers, of the chamber, a chamberlain's household name.
biblical_def: Richard Chambers preached no sermons and wrote no books. He was a layman of means who, through the whole of Mary's reign, carried and distributed the money that kept the scattered English congregations alive at Zurich, Strasbourg, Frankfurt, Basel and Geneva. He travelled between the cities, settled accounts, found lodging for students, and with Thomas Heton and others organised what amounted to a relief fund for an exiled church. Several of the exiles who afterward filled English pulpits and bishoprics had been fed in the meantime by his administration. The dictionary gives him an entry deliberately. A church in flight needs men who will handle money honestly and be in the right city on the right day, and Scripture dignifies that labour by name: the deacons were appointed to it, and Paul took pains to carry the collection for the poor saints in a way that no one could question. Chambers is the Marian exile who is invisible in the martyrologies and without whom a good part of the Elizabethan settlement's leadership would not have survived the 1550s.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines almoner as an officer who distributes alms, and treasurer as one who has the care of a treasure or of money.
webster_full: AL'MONER, n. An officer whose duty is to distribute charity or alms.
TREAS'URER, n. One who has the care of a treasure or of treasure; an officer who receives the public money.
STEW'ARD, n. A man employed to manage the affairs of another; one who has the care of another's property.
RELIE'F, n. The removal, in whole or in part, of any evil that afflicts the body or mind; succour.
scriptures: Act 6:3
Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.
Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men.
For it hath pleased them of Macedonia and Achaia to make a certain contribution for the poor saints which are at Jerusalem.
Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
corruption_summary: A layman who financed and administered the exiled English congregations through Mary's whole reign.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that the work which counts in the church is the work that is seen from the pulpit, so that money and administration are tolerated as a necessary dullness rather than honoured as a gift. Chambers did nothing else and the exile held together.

The principle to recover is that handling the church's money well is a spiritual office with a spiritual qualification. The Jerusalem church looked for “men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom” (Act 6:3) before it trusted anyone with a daily distribution. Paul's own practice was openly audited: “Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men” (2Co 8:21). And the one thing asked of such a man is the thing Chambers gave — “that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2).

pos: n. (Thomas Lever, c. 1521–1577, Marian exile at Aarau, afterwards Archdeacon of Coventry)
etymology: Aramaic Te'oma through Greek Thomas, a twin; English Lever, from Old English leofhere, dear army.
biblical_def: Thomas Lever was a Cambridge preacher of the Edwardian years whose sermons at Paul's Cross attacked the plunder of church lands and the starving of parishes by patrons who pocketed the tithes and left no stipend for a preacher. Under Mary he went abroad and settled with the small English company at Aarau in the Bernese territory, one of the quieter and poorer of the exile congregations. He came home at Elizabeth's accession, became Archdeacon of Coventry and master of Sherburn hospital, and went on saying the same thing: that a church with impropriated livings would have no ministry, and that the men who had taken the monastic revenues had not thereby reformed anything. The dictionary keeps him for that single clear note. Lever is the Marian exile who saw that a Reformation could be defeated not by persecution but by greed — that it is perfectly possible to pull down the mass, keep the money, and leave the parishes without the word.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines impropriate as to convert to private use, and tithe as the tenth part set aside for the support of the ministry.
webster_full: IMPRO'PRIATE, v.t. To convert to private use; to appropriate; as, to impropriate the tithes of a parish.
TITHE, n. The tenth part of the annual produce of land or of the increase of animals, devoted to the support of the ministry.
ARCHDE'ACON, n. An ecclesiastical dignitary next in rank below a bishop, who has jurisdiction over a part of the diocese.
SAC'RILEGE, n. The crime of violating or profaning sacred things; the alienating to common purposes what has been devoted to religion.
scriptures: Mal 3:8
Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings.
And I perceived that the portions of the Levites had not been given them: for the Levites and the singers, that did the work, were fled every one to his field.
Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel.
For the scripture saith, Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And, The labourer is worthy of his reward.
corruption_summary: He preached against the plunder of church livings and said a robbed parish would have no preaching.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the conviction that a reformation is finished when the doctrine has been corrected, while the money continues to run exactly as it did before. Lever's complaint was concrete: the tithes of a parish were being drawn by a lay owner who paid a stipend too small to keep a preacher, so that the pulpit stood empty under a Protestant settlement.

The principle to recover is that God counts the diversion of what was given to Him as theft, and that the ministry He commands must be paid for by the people who receive it. “Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me” (Mal 3:8). Nehemiah found the Levites gone back to their fields because their portions had not been given them, and his answer was not a sermon but a reckoning — “Why is the house of God forsaken?” (Neh 13:11). Paul settles the duty without embarrassment: “The labourer is worthy of his reward” (1Ti 5:18).

pos: n. (John Scory, d. 1585, Marian exile and superintendent of the English congregation at Emden, afterwards Bishop of Hereford)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan through Latin Johannes, the LORD is gracious; Scory, an English surname of uncertain origin.
biblical_def: John Scory had been a Dominican friar before the Reformation reached him, was made Bishop of Rochester and then of Chichester under Edward VI, and was deprived by Mary. He crossed to Emden in East Friesland, where a sizeable English colony had gathered, and acted as superintendent of their congregation, writing pastoral letters of comfort back to the faithful in England and seeing some translation work through the Emden presses. At Elizabeth's accession he returned and was given Hereford, a border diocese he held for twenty-six years. The dictionary records him with the honesty the record requires: a man who came the whole distance from the cloister to a Reformed pulpit, who in exile wrote to encourage prisoners he could not reach, and whose long tenure at Hereford drew complaints about his management of the see's property. Both things are true and the entry keeps both. Scory's letters to the persecuted belong with the best of that literature; the later complaints are a reminder that the Reformation's recovered gospel did not instantly reform every man who preached it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines superintendent as one who has the oversight and charge of something, and comfort as to strengthen and console.
webster_full: SUPERINTEND'ENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of some place, person or business, with the power of direction.
COM'FORT, v.t. To strengthen; to invigorate; to console or cheer in affliction.
FRI'AR, n. An appellation common to monks of all orders; a brother of a religious order.
EPIS'TLE, n. A writing communicated from one person to another; a letter.
scriptures: Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God.
For ye had compassion of me in my bonds, and took joyfully the spoiling of your goods, knowing in yourselves that ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance.
Phi 1:7
Even as it is meet for me to think this of you all, because I have you in my heart; inasmuch as both in my bonds, and in the defence and confirmation of the gospel, ye all are partakers of my grace.
Col 4:18
The salutation by the hand of me Paul. Remember my bonds. Grace be with you. Amen.
corruption_summary: A former friar turned Reformed bishop who wrote letters of comfort to the persecuted from exile at Emden.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern wish for unmixed subjects — either the heroic exile or the grasping prelate, and never the same man. Scory wrote to strangers in prison and he also quarrelled over the revenues of Hereford, and the dictionary names both because Scripture never flatters its own servants.

The principle to recover is that comfort is a ministry and not a mood, and that the comfort God gives is given in order to be handed on. He “comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble” (2Co 1:4). The Hebrews had done it in the flesh: they “took joyfully the spoiling of your goods” (Heb 10:34) for the sake of brethren in bonds. And Paul's shortest request, written in his own hand, is the whole of what an exile can send home — “Remember my bonds” (Col 4:18).

pos: n. (William Cole, c. 1530–1600, Marian exile at Zurich and Geneva, afterwards President of Corpus Christi College, Oxford)
etymology: Germanic Wilhelm, resolute protector; English Cole, from Old English col, coal, dark.
biblical_def: William Cole was a fellow of Corpus Christi who lost his place under Mary and spent the exile years at Zurich and then at Geneva, where he was among the English company that produced the Geneva Bible and served the congregation there. He came back in 1559, held parish and cathedral preferments, and in 1568 was imposed on Corpus Christi as President by royal mandate against the wishes of a largely conservative fellowship; he kept the office for thirty years and spent much of it in dispute with the men he governed. The dictionary records him as a working member of the Geneva company, the body of exiles whose annotated English Bible went into more English households over the next eighty years than any other book. Cole is not its famous name. He is one of the men who sat in Geneva doing collation and proof while Whittingham and Gilby got the credit, and the dictionary names him on the principle that the labour God sees is not the labour the title page records.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines annotation as a remark or note upon an author, and collate as to compare, to examine two things together.
webster_full: ANNOTA'TION, n. A remark, note or commentary on some passage of a book.
COLLA'TE, v.t. To lay together and compare, by examining the points in which two or more things of a similar kind agree or disagree.
VER'SION, n. A translation; that which is rendered from another language.
PRES'IDENT, n. An officer appointed to preside over a college or society.
scriptures: Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Pro 25:2
It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
corruption_summary: One of the working hands of the Geneva Bible company, named here because the title page does not name him.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the celebrity reading of church history, in which a translation has an author and the rest were assistants. The Geneva Bible was the work of a company, and the company was composed of deprived fellows living on charity in a foreign city, doing the slow collation that makes a readable English text possible.

The principle to recover is that God gives the sense of His word through plain labour and intends it to reach the plain hearer. The Levites “read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) — which is the whole aim of an annotated Bible. The Bereans show what such a text is for: they “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11). And the workman's rule is Paul's — “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15).

pos: n. (John Old, fl. 1545–1557, Marian exile, translator and controversialist against the papacy)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan through Latin Johannes, the LORD is gracious; English Old, from Old English eald, aged.
biblical_def: John Old was an Edwardian minister who worked at the business of putting learned Latin divinity into plain English, including a share in the English edition of the Paraphrases of Erasmus on the New Testament that Edward VI's government ordered set up in every parish church. Under Mary he fled to the Rhineland and from there wrote against the papacy, naming the Roman claim of universal headship as the usurpation it is. He died in exile. The dictionary keeps him for the pattern of his labour rather than the fame of it: a translator who believed the ploughman had a right to the arguments, and whose work was accordingly aimed at parishes rather than universities. The Reformation in England was carried as much by this kind of plain English printing as by the pulpit, and when Mary's council ordered such books burned it was paying the method a compliment. Old's controversial writing is severe, and the dictionary does not soften it: he judged that a church which had set a man in Christ's place over the conscience had unchurched itself, and he said so in English.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines paraphrase as an explanation of some text in other words more ample, and usurp as to seize without right.

USURP', v.t. To seize, take or hold in possession, by force or without right; as, to usurp a throne.

corruption_summary: He put Latin divinity into plain English for parishes, and named the papal headship as usurpation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a polite modern reluctance to say what the Reformers said about the papal office, as though the identification were merely a sixteenth-century temper rather than a judgment about where Christ's headship lies. Old's argument was not about the manners of any pope; it was that a man cannot be set between the conscience and God without displacing the one Mediator.

The principle to recover is the sole headship of Christ over His church and His sole mediation. The man of sin “exalteth himself above all that is called God” (2Th 2:4). Our Lord forbade the title outright: “be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren” (Mat 23:8). And the office is already filled — “he is the head of the body, the church” (Col 1:18); “there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5).

pos: n. (Thomas Cole, d. 1571, Marian exile at Frankfurt, afterwards Archdeacon of Essex)
etymology: Aramaic Te'oma through Greek Thomas, a twin; English Cole, from Old English col, coal, dark.
biblical_def: Thomas Cole had been master of Maidstone school and a preacher of the Edwardian reform before Mary drove him abroad, and he settled with the English congregation at Frankfurt — the congregation whose internal quarrel over the Prayer Book and the form of worship became the most bitter of the whole exile. He returned at Elizabeth's accession, was made Archdeacon of Essex and Dean of Salisbury's commissary, and preached at the opening of the 1561 convocation. The dictionary records him as a man of the middle of that quarrel, and takes the quarrel itself seriously rather than treating it as emigre bad temper. At Frankfurt the English church had to decide, without a queen to decide for it, what its worship would be; the division ran between those who held the Edwardian Prayer Book as a settled inheritance and those who wanted the simpler Reformed order they saw around them. Cole lived through it and came home to serve in the church that resulted, which is the ordinary and unglamorous end of most such disputes.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines schism as a division or separation in a church, and liturgy as a form of prayer prescribed for public worship.
webster_full: SCHISM, n. In a general sense, division or separation; in church affairs, a division of a church or denomination.
LIT'URGY, n. In a general sense, all public ceremonies that belong to divine service; a formulary of public devotions.
CONVOCA'TION, n. An assembly of the clergy, by their representatives, to consult on ecclesiastical affairs.
ARCHDE'ACON, n. An ecclesiastical dignitary next in rank below a bishop.

corruption_summary: He lived through the Frankfurt congregation's quarrel over worship and came home to serve the settled church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern assumption that a congregational dispute about worship is always a failure of charity, so that the only godly man in such a room is the one with no convictions. The Frankfurt exiles were arguing about a real question: whether a form of prayer is a settled inheritance to be defended or a thing to be revised toward the plainest Scriptural order.

The principle to recover is that unity is commanded and is commanded about something. Paul asks “that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10) — sameness of speech, not silence. The bond is to be kept with effort: “Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3). And the rule that ought to have governed Frankfurt governs still: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40).

pos: n. (John Mullins, d. 1591, Marian exile at Zurich, afterwards Archdeacon of London)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan through Latin Johannes, the LORD is gracious; English Mullins, from Old French moulin, a mill, a miller's family name.
biblical_def: John Mullins was a Magdalen man and a physician by training who went abroad under Mary and lived at Zurich among the English company that Bullinger sheltered. He came back at Elizabeth's accession, was made Archdeacon of London and a canon of St Paul's, and served in the capital's church courts and visitations for thirty years, examining candidates for the ministry and dealing with the parishes' disorder. The dictionary names him because the exile produced two sorts of returning men: the famous controversialists, and the administrators who had to make a reformed ministry out of the clergy actually available. Mullins belonged to the second sort. A diocese needs a man who will sit through the dull examination of a hundred candidates and decline the unfit, and the Reformation's recovery of preaching stood or fell on whether such men did their work. His long correspondence with the Zurich divines kept the English church in touch with the churches that had fed her in her poverty.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines visitation as the act of a superior examining into the state of a church, and examine as to search into and inquire.
webster_full: VISITA'TION, n. The act of visiting for inspection; the object or purpose of examining the state of a church or diocese.
EXAM'INE, v.t. To inspect carefully; to search or inquire into; to interrogate, as a witness or a candidate.
CAN'ON, n. A dignitary of the church; a member of a cathedral chapter.
OR'DINATION, n. The act of conferring holy orders or sacerdotal power.

And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
corruption_summary: An exile at Zurich who came home and spent thirty years examining candidates for the London ministry.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is an impatience with examination itself — the notion that testing a man before he is trusted with a pulpit is institutional caution rather than pastoral duty. Mullins had the harder half of the Elizabethan settlement: not writing what the ministry ought to be, but deciding, candidate by candidate, who would be allowed into it.

The principle to recover is that the church is commanded to prove men before she ordains them, and that haste here is sin. “And let these also first be proved” (1Ti 3:10). The warning is explicit: “Lay hands suddenly on no man” (1Ti 5:22). And the succession Paul describes is deliberately filtered — the things heard are to be committed “to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2).
